overview.title: 📖 Overview: Dedications, Their Destination, and a New Chapter on Sales
overview.subtitle: Arakhin 29a–29b
overview.hebrewSource: חֶרְמֵי כֹהֲנִים אֵין לָהֶן פִּדְיוֹן וְנִותָּנִין לַכֹּהֵן. חֲרָמִים כׇּל זְמַן שֶׁהֵן בְּבֵית בְּעָלִים הֲרֵי הֵן כְּהֶקְדֵּשׁ
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The Gemara continues examining ḥerem (dedication for the priests), tracking exactly when it behaves like ordinary consecrated property and when it becomes fully non-sacred, and revisiting the dispute over where an unspecified dedication defaults — Temple maintenance or the priests directly — through a real incident in Pumbedita. A baraita then raises the question of whether the laws of ḥerem even apply in an era without an active Jubilee. The daf closes its chapter and opens a new one on selling — not consecrating — a field, governed by its own Torah-mandated minimum holding period, and a sharp Rav-and-Shmuel dispute about a sale made during the Jubilee Year itself.

slides.title: 🪙 A Dedication's Two Legal Lives
slides.subtitle: Fully sacred in the owner's hands, fully ordinary once it reaches a priest
rows: Treated exactly like consecrated property (hekdesh) in every respect
'Every dedicated item is most sacred to the Lord' (Lev. 27:28)
Fully non-sacred, like any of his ordinary belongings
'Everything dedicated in Israel shall be yours' (Num. 18:14)
Unspecified dedication — R' Yehuda ben Beteira
Same verse, 'most sacred to the Lord'
'As a field dedicated, its possession shall be to the priest' (Lev. 27:21)

callout.label: A confusing ruling:
callout.text: Rav says the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira — but only once you realize that Rav's own version of the mishna and baraita swap which side holds which opinion. Untangling that swap is its own small sugya.

slides.title: 🌊 The Pumbedita Dedication: Redeem It, or Give It All Away?
slides.subtitle: A real case tests where an unspecified dedication really belongs

lines.speaker: The case
lines.text: A man in Pumbedita dedicated his property without specifying its purpose, then came to Rav Yehuda asking what to do.

lines.speaker: Rav Yehuda
lines.text: Take four dinars, transfer the property's sanctity onto them, then throw the dinars in the river (since no benefit may be taken from them) — and your property is redeemed and permitted to you.

lines.speaker: Implication
lines.text: This only works if unspecified dedications go to Temple maintenance, which can be redeemed — dedications to the priests directly could never be redeemed this way.

lines.speaker: Ulla
lines.text: 'Had I been there, I would have given it ALL to the priests' — meaning unspecified dedications go straight to the priests, with no possibility of redemption at all.

callout.label: Why only 4 dinars?
callout.text: Post-Temple, one may redeem hekdesh even for less than its true value — but Rav Yehuda still specified a real sum (not a single peruta) simply to publicize that a valid redemption had taken place.

slides.title: 🏛️ Does Ḥerem Still Apply Without an Active Jubilee?
slides.subtitle: A baraita seems to tie the whole institution to the Jubilee cycle

nodes.content: ❓ Baraita: the Hebrew slave, the dedicated ancestral field, and houses in walled cities all 'apply only in an era when the Jubilee is observed' — so does ḥerem stop functioning entirely today?
💡 Resolution: that baraita speaks only of land — dedicated fields, tied intrinsically to the Jubilee's return-cycle
✅ Movable property dedications remain fully in force always — which is exactly why the Pumbedita case (about property) still needed real redemption

callout.label: Related mishna:
callout.text: Rabbi Yishmael reconciles two verses on firstborn animals — 'you shall consecrate' (Deut. 15:19) and 'a man shall not consecrate it' (Lev. 27:26) — by distinguishing a 'consecration of value' (the right to give it to a chosen priest) from consecration for the altar, which is impossible since a firstborn already carries its own sanctity.

slides.title: 🌾 New Chapter: Selling (Not Consecrating) a Field
slides.subtitle: New mishna: a Torah-mandated waiting period before redemption

steps.content: 1️⃣ Base rule: a field sold while the Jubilee cycle is active cannot be redeemed less than two years after the sale — from the plural 'years' in Lev. 25:15
2️⃣ A year of blight, mildew, or the Sabbatical Year doesn't count toward that tally, since the buyer got no real benefit from it
3️⃣ But a year the buyer merely plowed (without sowing) or left fallow DOES count — the field was still fit to produce
4️⃣ Rabbi Eliezer: if sold full of produce just before Rosh Hashana, the buyer may end up eating three crops in those two years — payment is reckoned by years, not by harvests

callout.label: It's a prohibition, not just advice:
callout.text: The Gemara reads the mishna's 'not permitted to redeem' as a real prohibition — one may not even 'rattle coins' at the buyer to pressure an early sale. Both seller and buyer are bound by their own positive mitzvot from the same verse.

slides.title: 🔄 Selling a Field During the Jubilee Year Itself
slides.subtitle: Rav and Shmuel disagree sharply about whether such a sale has any effect

boxes.title: Rav: Sold, Then Reverts
items: The sale IS valid in principle
But the field immediately leaves the buyer's possession
The buyer's money is NOT refunded — he simply loses it

boxes.title: Shmuel: Never Sold At All
items: Kal vachomer: if a field already sold before the Jubilee reverts at the Jubilee, surely a field NOT yet sold cannot be newly sold during it
The sale has no effect whatsoever

callout.label: A parallel dilemma:
callout.text: Rav Anan recalled two similar rulings from Shmuel — this one, and a case of selling a Canaanite slave abroad — but couldn't remember which involved a refund. Rav Yosef resolves it from a baraita's own wording.

summary.principle: A dedication (ḥerem) remains fully consecrated only until it reaches the priest's hand, after which it becomes ordinary property; and separately, an ordinary field sale carries its own Torah-mandated minimum holding period, with land-sales during the Jubilee Year itself sparking a fundamental dispute over whether they take effect at all.

flowSteps.content: 🪙 Dedications: fully sacred in the owner's hands, fully ordinary once given to a priest
🌊 Unspecified dedications: Rav Yehuda treats them as redeemable (Temple maintenance); Ulla sends them straight to the priests

columns.content: 🏛️ Land-based ḥerem needs an active Jubilee; movable-property ḥerem applies always
🌾 A sold field needs 2 years before redemption; blight/Shvi'it years don't count, plowed/fallow years do

flowSteps.content: 🔄 Selling IN the Jubilee Year itself: Rav says sold-but-reverts (no refund); Shmuel says never sold (refund)
🎓 Key Principle: Jewish law tracks exactly when sanctity or ownership transfers, down to the specific moment and the specific year

quiz.q: According to the baraita, what is the status of a dedication (ḥerem) once the owner has actually given it to a priest?
o: It remains fully sacred forever
It becomes fully non-sacred, treated like any of the priest's ordinary property
It reverts automatically to the original owner
It must be destroyed
quiz.e: The Gemara derives from 'everything dedicated in Israel shall be yours' (Numbers 18:14) that once a dedication reaches a priest's possession, it becomes ordinary, non-sacred property in every respect.

quiz.q: What does Rav Yehuda's advice in the Pumbedita incident (redeem with four dinars, then discard them) imply about where an unspecified dedication is designated?
o: That it is designated for the priests directly, with no possibility of redemption
That it is designated for Temple maintenance (bedek habayit), which CAN be redeemed
That it is entirely invalid and requires no action
That it must be split evenly between priests and Levites
quiz.e: Since Rav Yehuda permitted the property to be redeemed and then used, this implies he held that an unspecified dedication defaults to Temple maintenance, which — unlike a dedication to the priests — can be redeemed.

quiz.q: How does the Gemara resolve the apparent contradiction between a baraita stating that dedicated fields, Hebrew slaves, and walled-city houses apply 'only when the Jubilee is observed' and the ongoing application of ḥerem laws generally?
o: It concludes that ḥerem no longer applies at all today
It explains that the baraita's limitation applies specifically to LAND-based dedications, while dedications of movable property remain in force at all times
It rejects the baraita as unreliable
It applies the limitation only to gentile-owned property
quiz.e: The Gemara distinguishes: the baraita's Jubilee-dependent limitation concerns dedicated fields (land), which are intrinsically tied to the Jubilee return-cycle, while movable property dedications remain fully operative regardless of whether the Jubilee is currently observed.

quiz.q: According to the new mishna, why does a year in which the buyer merely plowed (without sowing) or left the field fallow still count toward the two-year minimum before the seller may redeem it?
o: Because plowing automatically doubles the field's value
Because the field remained fit to produce a crop that year, unlike a year of blight or the Sabbatical Year when no real benefit was possible
Because Jewish law never distinguishes between types of years
Because the buyer forfeits his rights if he doesn't cultivate
quiz.e: The mishna counts a plowed-but-unsown or fallow year toward the tally because the field was still capable of producing a crop that year — unlike blight, mildew, or Sabbatical years, when the buyer genuinely received no benefit.

quiz.q: What is the core disagreement between Rav and Shmuel regarding a field sold DURING the Jubilee Year itself?
o: Rav says the sale is entirely invalid; Shmuel says it's valid and permanent
Rav says the sale is valid but the field immediately reverts with no refund; Shmuel says the sale never took effect at all and the money is refunded
Both agree the sale is invalid but disagree only about the refund
Both agree the sale is valid and permanent
quiz.e: Rav holds the sale is technically valid but the field leaves the buyer's possession immediately, with no refund of the purchase money; Shmuel, via an a fortiori inference, holds the sale never took effect at all, so the money must be returned.
